Vectors and Matrices

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, like a single data point with several features. A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers: a whole dataset stacked row by row, or the weights of a neural network layer.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of a vector as one customer described by [age, income, visits], and a matrix as a spreadsheet where every row is a customer and every column is a feature.

The Dot Product

The dot product multiplies matching entries and sums them, measuring how much two vectors point the same way. For a=[1,2,3], b=[4,5,6]: 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

To multiply A (m×n) by B (n×p), each output entry (i,j) is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. The result is m×p; the inner dimensions n must match.

Worked Example

A = [[1, 2],      B = 5634           [7, 8]]
AB[0][0] = 1*5 + 2*7 = 19
AB[0][1] = 1*6 + 2*8 = 22
AB[1][0] = 3*5 + 4*7 = 43
AB[1][1] = 3*6 + 4*8 = 50
AB = 19224350
📝 KEY IDEA

A neural network layer computes y = Wx + b: a matrix-vector product plus a bias. Stacking layers just chains matrix multiplications with nonlinearities between them.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: AB ≠ BA in general, and BA may not even be defined if shapes do not line up.

📊 FIGURE — two facts that get asked directly
🎯 EXAM TIP
AI = IA = A — the identity is the matrix version of multiplying by 1, and it is the one matrix that commutes with everything. And transposing a 3×2 gives a 2×3: the shape flips. Watch the order reversal in (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ, which is where marks usually go.

Vector Spaces and Linear Combinations

A linear combination scales each vector and adds them: c1*v1 + c2*v2 + .... The set of ALL such combinations is their span.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If two vectors point in different directions on a table, mixing them in every ratio reaches any point on the tabletop. That flat surface is their span.

Independence and Basis

Vectors are linearly independent if none can be built from the others. A basis is a minimal independent set that spans the whole space. Its size is the dimension.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Test independence by setting a linear combination to zero. If only all-zero coefficients work, they are independent; a nonzero solution means one vector is redundant.

Worked Example

Are [1,0], [0,1], [2,3] independent? In 2D at most 2 vectors can be independent, so the third is redundant: [2,3] = 2*[1,0] + 3*[0,1]. They span the plane but are NOT independent.

📝 KEY IDEA

The rank of a matrix is its number of linearly independent columns (equal to independent rows). It reveals the true dimensionality of the information it carries.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Many vectors does not mean high dimension. Ten copies of one direction still span only a 1D line; redundancy inflates count but not rank.

📊 FIGURE — how large a rank can be
🎯 EXAM TIP
The largest possible rank of a 5×3 matrix is 3, because rank cannot exceed min(rows, columns). The reason it is min and not something subtler is the theorem that row rank always equals column rank — so the smaller dimension is the binding constraint.
"},"AIM-MATH/ch1/s3":{"body":"

Special Directions

An eigenvector of A is a nonzero vector v whose direction is unchanged under A: Av = λv. The scalar λ is the eigenvalue, the amount v is stretched or shrunk.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Most vectors get rotated by a matrix. Eigenvectors are the stubborn ones that only get longer or shorter, keeping their line, like the axes a spinning object turns around.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Solve det(A − λI) = 0, the characteristic equation, for the eigenvalues. For each λ, solve (A − λI)v = 0 to find its eigenvectors.

Worked Example

A = 2003
det(A - λI) = (2-λ)(3-λ) = 0
Eigenvalues: λ = 2 and λ = 3
Eigenvector for λ=2: [1, 0]
Eigenvector for λ=3: [0, 1]
📝 KEY IDEA

For a covariance matrix, eigenvectors are the directions of greatest variance and eigenvalues are the variance amounts. This is exactly what PCA finds.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The zero vector is never an eigenvector. Eigenvectors must be nonzero; only their direction matters, so any nonzero scaling of one is also valid.

📊 FIGURE — solving det(A − λI) = 0
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Working the characteristic equation

For A = [[5, 2], [2, 5]]:

det(A − λI) = (5 − λ)(5 − λ) − (2)(2) = (5 − λ)² − 4 = 0

So (5 − λ)² = 4, giving 5 − λ = ±2 and therefore λ = 3 and λ = 7.

Two sanity checks worth doing every time:

  • Trace = sum of eigenvalues: 5 + 5 = 10 = 7 + 3 ✓
  • Determinant = product: 25 − 4 = 21 = 7 × 3 ✓

The eigenvectors are [1, 1] for λ = 7 and [1, −1] for λ = 3 — orthogonal, which is guaranteed for any symmetric matrix.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Check eigenvalues against the trace (their sum) and the determinant (their product) before committing — for [[5,2],[2,5]] that is 10 and 21, satisfied by 7 and 3. It catches sign slips in seconds. Symmetric matrices additionally guarantee real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors.

Orthogonality

Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, meeting at a right angle. A set is orthonormal if mutually orthogonal and each of length 1.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Projecting a vector onto a line is the shadow it casts straight down onto that line under a noon sun: the closest point on the line to the original.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The projection of b onto a is (a·b / a·a) a. The leftover b − proj is orthogonal to a: the error you cannot capture along a.

Least Squares

When Ax = b has no exact solution, we minimize squared error. The solution satisfies the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b, projecting b onto A's column space.

Worked Example

Project b=[2,2] onto a=[1,0]:
a·b = 2*1 + 2*0 = 2,  a·a = 1
proj = (2/1)*[1,0] = [2,0]
error = b - proj = [0,2]  (orthogonal to a)
📝 KEY IDEA

Linear regression IS least squares: it projects the target onto the space spanned by the feature columns, minimizing squared residuals.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Least squares minimizes the SUM OF SQUARED errors, not absolute errors, which is why it is sensitive to outliers.

Singular Value Decomposition

Any matrix A factors as A = U Σ V^T. U and V are orthogonal (rotations/reflections) and Σ is diagonal with nonnegative singular values ordered largest to smallest.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

SVD says every linear transformation is really: rotate, stretch along axes, rotate again. The singular values are the stretch amounts.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

PCA centers the data, then finds the top directions of variance: the top right-singular vectors of the data matrix (equivalently, eigenvectors of the covariance matrix). Projecting onto the first k reduces dimensions while keeping most variance.

Worked Example

Suppose singular values are 5, 4, 1. Total energy is 5^2+4^2+1^2 = 42. Keeping the top two captures (25+16)/42 ≈ 98% of variance, so dropping the third loses ~2%.

📝 KEY IDEA

Truncating SVD to the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation of a matrix, the foundation of image compression, recommenders, and PCA.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

PCA is scale-sensitive: features on larger numeric scales dominate variance. Standardize first, or the largest-unit feature hijacks the top components.

What a Derivative Measures

The derivative of f at a point is the slope of the tangent line: how fast the output changes as the input nudges. We write f'(x) or df/dx.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

If f(x) is your position over time, f'(x) is your speedometer reading at that instant, the rate right now, not the average over the whole trip.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Power rule: d/dx[x^n] = n·x^(n-1). Chain rule: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f'(g(x)) · g'(x). You multiply the outer rate by the inner rate.

Worked Example

f(x) = (3x + 1)^2
Let g = 3x+1, so f = g^2
f'(x) = 2g * g' = 2(3x+1) * 3 = 6(3x+1)
At x=1: f'(1) = 6*4 = 24
📝 KEY IDEA

Deep networks are deeply nested functions. Training uses the chain rule to multiply local derivatives layer by layer; that chained product is exactly backpropagation.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Forgetting the inner derivative. d/dx[sin(2x)] is 2cos(2x), NOT cos(2x): the factor of 2 from inside is required by the chain rule.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch2/s2":{"body":"

Partial Derivatives

When a function has several inputs, a partial derivative measures its rate of change with respect to ONE variable while holding the others fixed. We write ∂f/∂x.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

On a hillside, the partial in the east direction is how steep the ground is if you walk only east. The gradient combines all such slopes into one arrow pointing straight uphill.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The gradient ∇f is the vector of all partial derivatives. It points in the direction of steepest ascent, and its magnitude is how steep that ascent is.

Worked Example

f(x, y) = x^2 + 3xy
∂f/∂x = 2x + 3y   (treat y as constant)
∂f/∂y = 3x        (treat x as constant)
Gradient at (1, 2): ∇f = [2+6, 3] = [8, 3]
📝 KEY IDEA

To minimize a loss we step in the direction of the NEGATIVE gradient, steepest descent, because that reduces the function fastest.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The gradient points uphill (ascent), not downhill. Gradient descent must negate it. A zero gradient marks a critical point but not necessarily a minimum.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch2/s3":{"body":"

Finding and Classifying Extrema

To optimize a multivariable function, first find critical points where the gradient is zero, then classify each using curvature from the Hessian, the matrix of second partial derivatives.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A critical point is anywhere the ground is flat: the bottom of a valley (min), the top of a hill (max), or a mountain pass (saddle) that goes up one way and down another.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

At a critical point, a positive-definite Hessian (all eigenvalues > 0) means a local minimum; all eigenvalues < 0 means a maximum; mixed signs mean a saddle point.

Worked Example

f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2
∇f = [2x, 2y] = 0  at  (0,0)
Hessian = 2002, eigenvalues 2,2 > 0
=> (0,0) is a local (and global) minimum
📝 KEY IDEA

In high-dimensional network loss surfaces, saddle points, not bad local minima, are the dominant obstacle that slows gradient descent.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A zero gradient alone does NOT confirm a minimum. Without checking curvature you might be at a maximum or a saddle where training stalls.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch2/s4":{"body":"

Learning by Gradients

Training a network means adjusting weights to reduce a loss. The forward pass computes predictions and loss; the backward pass (backpropagation) computes how the loss changes with each weight.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Backprop is like assigning blame. After a wrong answer it works backward asking each weight, 'how much did you contribute to the error?' and nudges it accordingly.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Backprop applies the chain rule from the loss backward, reusing each layer's local gradient. Each weight updates by w ← w − η · ∂L/∂w, where η is the learning rate.

Worked Example

Loss L = (y_pred - y)^2,  y_pred = w*x
∂L/∂y_pred = 2(y_pred - y)
∂y_pred/∂w = x
∂L/∂w = 2(y_pred - y) * x   (chain rule)
Update: w ← w - η * ∂L/∂w
📝 KEY IDEA

Backprop is an efficient, ordered application of the chain rule that reuses intermediate results, so gradients for millions of parameters cost about one extra forward pass.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A learning rate too large makes updates overshoot and diverge; too small makes training crawl. It scales the gradient step and must be tuned.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch3/s1":{"body":"

Random Variables and Distributions

A random variable takes values with certain probabilities. A distribution assigns those probabilities. Discrete variables (a die roll) use a probability mass function; continuous ones (a height) use a density.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Expectation is the long-run average if you repeated the experiment forever. Variance measures how spread out outcomes are around that average: small means predictable, large means erratic.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Expectation: E[X] = Σ x·P(x). Variance: Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])^2] = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2. The standard deviation is its square root.

Worked Example

Fair die: values 1..6 each prob 1/6
E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5
E[X^2] = (1+4+9+16+25+36)/6 = 91/6 ≈ 15.17
Var(X) = 15.17 - 3.5^2 = 15.17 - 12.25 ≈ 2.92
📝 KEY IDEA

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is central to ML: noise models, weight initializations, and the Central Limit Theorem all rely on it.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Variance is in squared units. To compare spread on the original scale, use the standard deviation, not the variance itself.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch3/s2":{"body":"

Updating Beliefs

Bayes' theorem revises a probability given evidence: P(H|E) = P(E|H)·P(H) / P(E). The prior P(H) is belief before evidence; the likelihood P(E|H) is how well H explains the evidence; the posterior P(H|E) is the updated belief.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

You start with a hunch (prior). Evidence arrives. Bayes tells you exactly how much to shift it: strong evidence moves it a lot, weak evidence barely at all.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Multiply prior by likelihood, then normalize by the total probability of the evidence. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) instead picks parameters that make the observed data most probable.

Worked Example

Disease affects 1% (prior). Test 90% sensitive,
8% false positive.
P(pos)=0.9*0.01 + 0.08*0.99 = 0.009+0.0792=0.0882
P(disease|pos)=0.009/0.0882 ≈ 0.102 (~10%)

Even a positive test leaves only ~10% chance of disease, because it is rare.

📝 KEY IDEA

Training many ML models is MLE (or MAP): minimizing cross-entropy loss is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the training labels.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The base-rate fallacy: ignoring the prior. A positive test on a rare condition can still mean low probability, as the example shows.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch3/s3":{"body":"

Memoryless Processes

A Markov chain models a system moving among states where the next state depends ONLY on the current state, not the full history. This is the Markov property.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Tomorrow's weather depends on today's, not last week's. A Markov chain forgets the past beyond the present state; the present holds all the information you need.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A transition matrix P holds probabilities P[i][j] of moving from state i to state j; each row sums to 1. From distribution x, one step gives xP, and n steps give xP^n.

Worked Example

States Sunny/Rainy. P = 0.80.20.40.6
Start Sunny x=[1,0].
After one step: xP = [0.8, 0.2]
After two steps: [0.8,0.2]P = [0.72, 0.28]
📝 KEY IDEA

Many chains converge to a stationary distribution π satisfying πP = π. PageRank, MCMC sampling, and reinforcement learning all rest on Markov dynamics.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

In the row-vector convention, rows (not columns) of the transition matrix must sum to 1. Mixing up the convention flips which dimension normalizes.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch3/s4":{"body":"

Testing Claims with Data

Hypothesis testing asks whether observed data is surprising under a default assumption, the null hypothesis (H0). The alternative (H1) is what we suspect instead.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

It works like a courtroom: the null hypothesis is innocent by default. We only convict (reject H0) if the evidence would be very unlikely for an innocent defendant.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming H0 is true. If p is below a threshold α (often 0.05) we reject H0. A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values.

Worked Example

New model beats old by 3% accuracy.
H0: no real difference. Test yields p = 0.02.
Since 0.02 < 0.05, reject H0:
the improvement is statistically significant.
📝 KEY IDEA

Reporting uncertainty (confidence intervals, error bars) on model metrics matters as much as the point estimate: a 1% gain within noise is not real progress.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A p-value is NOT the probability that H0 is true, and a non-significant result does not prove H0. Testing many hypotheses inflates false positives.

📊 FIGURE — why 10 tests at 0.05 is not a 5% risk
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The 40% you did not sign up for

Each independent test at α = 0.05 has a 95% chance of not producing a false positive. Across ten of them:

P(no false positive) = 0.95¹⁰ = 0.5987

P(at least one) = 1 − 0.5987 = 0.4013 ≈ 40%

So running ten tests at the usual threshold gives roughly a two-in-five chance of a spurious "significant" result.

Bonferroni divides the family-wise rate by the number of tests:

0.05 / 10 = 0.005

It is conservative — it protects the family-wise rate at the cost of power. When you are screening hundreds of hypotheses and can tolerate some false discoveries, Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate instead and keeps more power.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The Bonferroni-corrected threshold for 10 tests at a family-wise rate of 0.05 is 0.005 — divide α by the number of tests. Know the motivating number too: ten uncorrected tests carry about a 40% chance of at least one false positive, which is the reason the correction exists.

Descending the Loss

Gradient descent minimizes a loss by stepping opposite the gradient: θ ← θ − η·∇L(θ). The learning rate η controls step size.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine hiking downhill in fog. You feel the slope underfoot and step downhill. The learning rate is your stride: too long and you overshoot the valley, too short and you barely move.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Batch GD uses the full dataset per step (accurate but slow). Stochastic GD (SGD) uses one example (noisy but fast). Mini-batch GD uses a small batch, balancing stability and speed, the deep learning standard.

Worked Example

Minimize L(θ)=θ^2. ∇L = 2θ. η=0.1, start θ=5.
Step1: θ = 5 - 0.1*10 = 4
Step2: θ = 4 - 0.1*8  = 3.2
Step3: θ = 3.2 - 0.1*6.4 = 2.56 ...  → 0
📝 KEY IDEA

SGD's noise is a feature: it helps escape shallow saddle points and lets training process massive datasets one small batch at a time.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Too large a learning rate can make the loss oscillate or diverge; too small wastes compute. Learning-rate tuning or schedules are essential.

📊 FIGURE — the vocabulary of a training loop
🎯 EXAM TIP
With 10,000 examples and a mini-batch of 100 there are 100 parameter updates in one epoch — steps per epoch is simply N ÷ batch size. The relationship worth carrying: halving the batch size doubles the number of updates per epoch, which is why batch size and learning rate are usually tuned together.
"},"AIM-MATH/ch4/s2":{"body":"

Why Convexity Matters

A function is convex if the segment between any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph. Equivalently it curves upward everywhere (non-negative second derivative).

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A convex loss is a single smooth bowl. Drop a marble anywhere and it rolls to the one lowest point. A non-convex loss is a bumpy landscape with many dips to get stuck in.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

For a convex function, any local minimum is automatically the global minimum, and gradient descent converges to it with a suitable step size. A set is convex if it contains the segment between any two of its points.

Worked Example

f(x) = x^2 is convex: f''(x) = 2 ≥ 0 everywhere.
Check midpoint of x=-2 and x=2:
f(-2)=4, f(2)=4, average = 4
f(0) = 0 ≤ 4  (graph lies below the chord)
📝 KEY IDEA

Linear and logistic regression with standard losses are convex, so they have unique solutions. Deep networks are non-convex, which is why initialization and optimizer choice matter.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Convexity rules out bad local minima but does NOT guarantee fast convergence: a poorly conditioned convex problem can still be slow without scaling or preconditioning.

📊 FIGURE — what you can do to convex functions
🎯 EXAM TIP
Of the usual options, max(f, g) is the one guaranteed convex — its epigraph is the intersection of two convex epigraphs, and intersections of convex sets are convex. Minimum, difference and product can all fail. This is why hinge loss (a max) and sums of convex losses stay convex, keeping the optimisation well behaved.
"},"AIM-MATH/ch4/s3":{"body":"

Penalizing Complexity

Regularization adds a penalty on large weights to the loss, discouraging overly complex models that memorize noise. This improves generalization to new data.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Regularization is a simplicity tax. The model can still fit the data, but it pays a fee for every unit of weight, so it prefers the simplest explanation that works.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

L2 (Ridge) adds λ·Σwi^2, shrinking weights smoothly toward zero. L1 (Lasso) adds λ·Σ|wi|, driving many weights exactly to zero, producing sparse feature-selecting models.

Worked Example

Loss = MSE + λ * penalty
Weights w = [3, 0.1, -2]
L2 penalty = 3^2 + 0.1^2 + (-2)^2 = 9+0.01+4 = 13.01
L1 penalty = |3| + |0.1| + |-2| = 5.1
Larger λ => stronger shrinkage toward zero.
📝 KEY IDEA

L1 yields sparse, interpretable models by zeroing weights; L2 keeps all features but small. Elastic Net combines both. The strength λ trades bias against variance.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Too much regularization (λ too high) underfits: the model becomes too simple and biased. Too little overfits. λ must be tuned, typically by validation.

"},"AIM-MATH/ch4/s4":{"body":"

Beyond Plain SGD

Modern optimizers accelerate and stabilize training. Momentum accumulates a running average of past gradients, smoothing the path and speeding through ravines. Adaptive methods give each parameter its own effective learning rate.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Plain SGD is a hiker taking fixed steps. Momentum is a heavy ball rolling downhill that builds speed and ignores little bumps. Adam adds smart braking on steep, jittery directions.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Adam keeps two running averages: the first moment (mean of gradients, like momentum) and the second moment (mean of squared gradients). It divides the step by the square root of the second moment, so large, noisy gradients take smaller steps.

Worked Example

Momentum: v ← β·v + (1-β)·g ,  θ ← θ - η·v
With β=0.9, past velocity persists 90% each step,
so consistent gradient directions accumulate speed
while oscillating directions cancel out.
📝 KEY IDEA

Adam = momentum (1st moment) + RMSProp-style per-parameter scaling (2nd moment) + bias correction. It is a default optimizer for much of deep learning because it needs little tuning.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Adam is not universally best: for some tasks well-tuned SGD with momentum generalizes better. Adam still needs a reasonable base learning rate; it is adaptive, not tuning-free.

Linear Algebra Reference

💡 KEY RESULTS

Spectral theorem: a real symmetric A is orthogonally diagonalizable, A=QΛQᵀ with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors. SVD: any A=UΣVᵀ; σᵢ=√(λᵢ(AᵀA)); rank = # nonzero σ. Rank–nullity: rank+nullity=n. A is positive definite ⇔ all eigenvalues >0 ⇔ all leading principal minors >0.

⚙️ FORMULAS

det A = Πλᵢ, tr A = Σλᵢ. 2-norm condition number κ₂(A)=σ_max/σ_min. Orthogonal projector onto col(A): P=A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ, P²=P=Pᵀ, tr P = rank. Rank-1 projector onto unit u: uuᵀ. ‖A‖_F²=Σσᵢ², ‖A‖₂=σ_max. Rayleigh quotient xᵀAx/xᵀx∈[λ_min,λ_max].

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

Characteristic polynomial det(A−λI)=0 gives eigenvalues; for 2×2 use λ²−(tr)λ+det=0. Geometric multiplicity = dim null(A−λI) ≤ algebraic multiplicity. Best rank-k approx (Eckart–Young): truncate SVD; error ‖A−A_k‖₂=σ_{k+1}.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Defective matrices (geometric < algebraic multiplicity) are NOT diagonalizable, e.g. 3103. Nonsymmetric matrices may have complex eigenvalues even when real; eigenvectors need not be orthogonal. Singular values ≠ |eigenvalues| unless A is symmetric PSD.

"},"AIM-MATH/intensive/s2":{"body":"

Matrix & Multivariable Calculus

💡 KEY RESULTS

Denominator layout: gradient is a column vector, Jacobian J has Jᵢⱼ=∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ. Hessian H=∇²f is symmetric for C² functions (Schwarz). A stationary point is a local min if H≻0, a local max if H≺0, and a saddle if H is indefinite. The gradient always points in the direction of steepest ascent, and is orthogonal to level sets.

⚙️ FORMULAS

∇(aᵀx)=a, ∇(xᵀx)=2x, ∇(xᵀAx)=(A+Aᵀ)x (=2Ax if A symmetric), Hessian =A+Aᵀ. ∇‖Ax−b‖²=2Aᵀ(Ax−b). Chain rule: ∇(g∘f)=Jfᵀ∇g. Directional derivative D_u f=∇fᵀu (u unit). d/dX tr(AX)=Aᵀ, d/dX tr(XᵀAX)=(A+Aᵀ)X, d/dX log det X = X⁻ᵀ.

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

Lagrange multipliers: at a constrained extremum ∇f=Σλᵢ∇gᵢ. Second-order Taylor: f(x+p)≈f(x)+∇fᵀp+½pᵀHp. To differentiate matrix expressions, expand to scalar sums or use the differential df=tr(Gᵀ dX) ⇒ ∂f/∂X=G.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

For nonsymmetric A, ∇(xᵀAx)=(A+Aᵀ)x, NOT 2Ax. H≻0 is sufficient but not necessary for a strict local min (e.g. x⁴ at 0). A vanishing gradient with indefinite Hessian is a saddle, not an extremum.

Probability, Statistics & Information Theory

💡 KEY RESULTS

MLE maximizes log-likelihood; MAP adds a log-prior (Gaussian prior ⇒ ridge/L2 penalty, Laplace prior ⇒ L1). An estimator's MSE = bias² + variance. KL(p‖q)≥0 with equality iff p=q (Gibbs); it is asymmetric. Cross-entropy H(p,q)=H(p)+KL(p‖q), so cross-entropy loss upper-bounds the true entropy. Mutual information I(X;Y)=KL(p(x,y)‖p(x)p(y))≥0 measures statistical dependence and vanishes iff X⊥Y.

⚙️ FORMULAS

Gaussian KL: KL(N(μ₀,σ₀²)‖N(μ₁,σ₁²))=log(σ₁/σ₀)+(σ₀²+(μ₀−μ₁)²)/(2σ₁²)−½. Chebyshev: P(|X−μ|≥kσ)≤1/k². Markov: P(X≥a)≤E[X]/a. Var(X)=E[X²]−(E[X])². Uniform(0,1): E=½, Var=1/12. Fisher info Bernoulli =1/(p(1−p)).

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

MLE: set d/dθ Σ log p(xᵢ;θ)=0. Gaussian variance MLE is σ̂²=(1/n)Σ(xᵢ−x̄)², biased low; the 1/(n−1) version is unbiased. Use Jensen E[g(X)]≥g(E[X]) for convex g to prove KL≥0.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

KL is not a metric (asymmetric, no triangle inequality). Uncorrelated ≠ independent (e.g. X and X² for symmetric X have covariance 0 but are dependent). The MLE variance is biased; dividing by n−1 (Bessel) restores unbiasedness.

Convex Optimization — Theory & Convergence

💡 KEY RESULTS

f convex ⇔ (C²) ∇²f⪰0 everywhere ⇔ f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)ᵀ(y−x). Strong convexity (m): ∇²f⪰mI. L-smoothness: ∇f is L-Lipschitz ⇔ ∇²f⪯LI. Condition number κ=L/m governs GD speed. For convex problems with Slater's condition, strong duality holds (zero duality gap).

⚙️ FORMULAS

GD step η on m-strongly-convex, L-smooth f: with η=1/L the error contracts by factor (1−m/L) per step (linear). Optimal η=2/(L+m) gives factor (κ−1)/(κ+1). Plain convex L-smooth: f(x_k)−f*≤L‖x₀−x*‖²/(2k) (O(1/k)). Divergence if η>2/L. Prox of λ‖·‖₁ = soft-threshold sign(x)max(|x|−λ,0).

📝 PROOF TECHNIQUE

KKT (convex, differentiable): stationarity ∇f+Σλᵢ∇gᵢ+Σνⱼ∇hⱼ=0, primal/dual feasibility, complementary slackness λᵢgᵢ=0, λᵢ≥0. For quadratics f=½xᵀAx−bᵀx the minimizer is x*=A⁻¹b, minimum −½bᵀA⁻¹b.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Convexity requires ∇²f⪰0 (PSD), not strict. x³ is not convex on R. A large κ makes GD slow — Nesterov acceleration improves iteration count from O(κ) to O(√κ). The L1 ball's corners lie on axes, promoting sparsity; the rotationally symmetric L2 ball does not.

SVD, Pseudoinverse & Matrix Calculus

Every real A (m×n) factors as A = UΣVᵀ with orthogonal U,V and non-negative diagonal Σ. Singular values σᵢ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse is A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ, giving the minimum-norm least-squares solution x = A⁺b.

💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Spectral 2-norm: ‖A‖₂ = σ_max; Frobenius: ‖A‖_F = √(Σσᵢ²) = √tr(AᵀA).
  • Spectral radius ρ(A) ≤ ‖A‖ for any induced norm, with equality only for normal matrices.
  • Rayleigh quotient R(x)=xᵀMx/xᵀx ranges over [λ_min, λ_max] for symmetric M.
  • Kronecker: eig(A⊗B) = {λᵢμⱼ}, and (A⊗B)(C⊗D)=AC⊗BD.
⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Sherman–Morrison: (A+uvᵀ)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ − (A⁻¹uvᵀA⁻¹)/(1+vᵀA⁻¹u).
  • Woodbury: (A+UCV)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ − A⁻¹U(C⁻¹+VA⁻¹U)⁻¹VA⁻¹.
  • ∇_X log det X = X⁻ᵀ; ∇_X tr(AXB) = AᵀBᵀ; ∇_X tr(XᵀAX)=(A+Aᵀ)X.
📝 TECHNIQUE

Backprop is matrix calculus: for y=Wx, if δ=∂L/∂y then ∂L/∂W = δxᵀ and ∂L/∂x = Wᵀδ. Chain rule composes Jacobians right-to-left; reverse-mode accumulates vᵀJ products cheaply.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

A matrix is positive definite iff all leading principal minors are positive (Sylvester) — checking only the diagonal or the determinant is insufficient. Also ρ(A) can be far below ‖A‖₂ for non-normal A, so small spectral radius does not bound transient growth.

Exponential Families, Information & Convex Optimization

An exponential family has density p(x|η)=h(x)exp(ηᵀT(x)−A(η)), where T(x) is the sufficient statistic and A(η) the log-partition. Cumulants come from A: ∇A(η)=E[T(x)], ∇²A(η)=Cov[T(x)], which is also the Fisher information in the natural parameterization.

💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Fisher information: I(θ)=E[(∂_θ log p)²]=−E[∂²_θ log p]; Cramér–Rao: Var(θ̂) ≥ 1/I(θ).
  • Jensen: for convex φ, φ(E[X]) ≤ E[φ(X)]; hence E[log X] ≤ log E[X].
  • Hoeffding: for X∈[a,b], P(|X̄−μ|≥t) ≤ 2exp(−2nt²/(b−a)²).
  • Natural gradient: ∇̃L = F⁻¹∇L — steepest descent in KL geometry, parameterization-invariant.
⚙️ FORMULAS
  • Bernoulli(p): I(p)=1/(p(1−p)); Poisson(λ): I(λ)=1/λ.
  • KL(N(μ₁,σ²)‖N(μ₂,σ²)) = (μ₁−μ₂)²/(2σ²).
  • Lagrangian L(x,λ)=f(x)+λᵀg(x); dual d(λ)=inf_x L; weak duality d*≤p*.
📝 TECHNIQUE

EM maximizes the ELBO L(q,θ)=E_q[log p(x,z)]+H(q). The E-step sets q=posterior p(z|x,θ), making the bound tight (KL=0); the M-step maximizes over θ. Each step never decreases the true log-likelihood.

⚠️ SUBTLETY

Strong duality (d*=p*) needs a constraint qualification — Slater's condition (a strictly feasible point) for convex problems — it is not automatic. For SGD, the O(1/√T) rate holds for convex non-smooth objectives; strong convexity plus decaying steps buys O(1/T).

📊 FIGURE — a concentration bound you can compute
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Computing the bound

Substituting n = 100 and t = 0.1 into P(|X̄ − μ| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−2nt²):

2·exp(−2 × 100 × 0.1²) = 2·exp(−2 × 100 × 0.01) = 2·exp(−2)

= 2 × 0.13534 = 0.2707 ≈ 0.271

Read it correctly: this is an upper bound on the probability of being off by 0.1 or more, not the probability itself. Hoeffding makes no distributional assumption beyond boundedness, which is what makes it both widely applicable and loose.

Note the exponent's shape: t appears squared and n linearly, so halving the tolerance you want costs four times the samples.

🎯 EXAM TIP
For n = 100 in [0,1] and t = 0.1, Hoeffding gives 2e⁻² ≈ 0.271. Two things to keep straight: it is an upper bound rather than an exact probability, and because the exponent is −2nt², tightening the tolerance by half requires four times as many samples.

Formulas & method

These problems use the core linear-algebra and calculus tools behind machine learning.

Matrix-vector product

For a 2×2 matrix and vector, each output entry is a row dotted with the vector: (Ax)ᵢ = Σⱼ Aᵢⱼ xⱼ. Example: 1234·[2,1] = [1·2+2·1, 3·2+4·1] = [4, 10].

Eigenvalues of a 2×2

Solve det(A − λI) = 0. For a triangular matrix the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries. For a symmetric abba they are a+b and a−b.

Dot product & cosine similarity

a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ. Cosine similarity = (a·b) / (‖a‖ ‖b‖), where ‖a‖ = √(Σ aᵢ²).

Gradients

∇f lists the partial derivatives. For f(x,y)=x²+y², ∇f=(2x, 2y). Evaluate at the given point.

Gradient-descent update

x_new = x − η∇f, subtracting the step size η times the gradient element-wise.

Activation derivatives

Sigmoid: σ' = σ(1−σ). Tanh: tanh' = 1 − tanh². ReLU: 1 for positive input, 0 otherwise. Each is written in terms of the activation's own value, so if you know the output you can get the slope directly.

Formulas & method

These problems cover the probability and loss functions used to train and evaluate models. All information quantities here use logarithm base 2, so the units are bits.

Expectation & variance

E[X] = Σ xᵢ pᵢ. Variance = E[X²] − (E[X])². For a Bernoulli variable with success probability p, Var = p(1−p).

Softmax

softmax(z)ᵢ = e^(zᵢ) / Σⱼ e^(zⱼ). Exponentiate each score, then divide by the total.

Entropy (base 2)

H = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ, measured in bits. A uniform distribution over n outcomes has entropy log₂ n.

Cross-entropy (base 2)

CE = −Σ pᵢ log₂ qᵢ, where p is the true distribution and q the predicted one. For a one-hot true label, CE = −log₂(q of the true class).

Bayes posterior

P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / [P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|¬D)P(¬D)]. Combine the likelihood and prior, then normalize.

Regression error

MSE = mean of squared errors, MAE = mean of absolute errors, both averaged over the vector entries. Useful reference: log₂ 0.25 = −2 and log₂ 0.5 = −1.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
